# Stylized Facts about AI Capabilities

Genesis of this work.

: In summer 2024 OpenAI was preparing to launch the first reasoning model (strawberry/o1-preview), I was asked to help estimate the likely economic impact.

      The new model performed far better on reasoning-intensive tasks (MATH, GPQA), comparable to a PhD student. What will be the impact of a model with PhD-level intelligence?

      Ideal: plug a vector of capabilities into an economic model, & predict change in equilibrium.

<!-- There is no standard economic model which I could plug this into to estimate the impact. -->


#  Stylized Facts and Implications

| Fact about AI                                            | Implication for Economics of AI             |
| -------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| 1. We have no standard metric for computer intelligence  | Opportunity for theorists.                  |
| 2. LLM capabilities are highly correlated.               | Directed technical change may be difficult. |
| 3. LLM capabilities are growing rapidly.                 | Diffusion isn't primary cause of growth.    |
| 4. LLM capabilities are distinct from human capabilites. | Need a two-factor model of ability.         |
| 5. There is no consensus on the bottleneck.              | Opportunity for theorists.                  |
| 6. Inference prices are falling at 10X/year.             | GDP share of compute may be small.                                             |
| 7. LLMs can either do a task cheaply or not at all.      | Unlikely to be equilibrium task-sharing     |



# We have no standard metric for computer intelligence.

**A graveyard of measures of human intelligence:**

| Measure          | Interpretation                                                                       | Year Passed |
| ---------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ---- |
| Chess            | Shannon: *"Chess is generally considered to require ‘thinking’ for skilful play."*   | 1997 |
| Winograd | *"when people pass the test, we would say they were thinking."*                      | 2019 |
| ARC-AGI          | *"the only formal benchmark of AGI progress."*                                       | 2024 |
| MMMU             | *"Benchmark for Expert AGI."*                                                        | 2025 |
| AGIEval          | *"general abilities ... in tasks pertinent to human cognition"* | 2025 |

      

There are some live proposals, none are canonical.
:    - @morris2023levels (Google DeepMind) five "levels of AGI."
     - OpenAI five "levels of AGI," not officially released.
     - @hendrycks2025agidefinition "the definition of AGI."

      Most definitions are either overly narrow or ambiguous.

This is a hard problem!

: It's intellectual quicksand, many smart people have got themselves stuck. Sensible to tread carefully.


# Available Metrics of AI capability

Two common metrics of AI capability.
:     1. **Scores on benchmarks.** There are hundreds of different benchmarks, however no canonical set, and they often get "saturated" relatively quickly. Continual scramble to create new benchmarks.

      1. **User pairwise preference.** Given two answers to a query, which do you prefer?  These are used by labs to measure user utility, also some 3rd-party data sources, esp. LMsys chatbot arena.

Other metrics of AI capability.
:     1. **Causal effect on user retention.** Used by labs but the results are not generally reported.
      2. **Uplift effects on human productivity.** Hard to compare over time because you need the same humans.
      3. **User willingness to pay.** Few studies, Brynjolfsson reports $100/user/month.
      4. **Adoption.** Hard to infer value.


# LLM capabilities are growing rapidly


Benchmarks are falling rapidly.

: It typically takes 18 months for LLM scores on a benchmark to go from 25% to 75%.
: ![](images/image7.png){width=5cm}

User preference scores are growing rapidly.

: Models have 70% win-rate over 1yo models (150 Elo/year).
: ![](images/2025-10-22-08-46-02.png){width=5cm}


# Implication for Economic Forecasts

There are many recent forecasts of AI's economic impact.
: Economists typically forecast 0-1.5% range, AI people typically 3-30%+.
   
      ![](images/2025-10-23-04-50-05.png){width=5cm}

# Implication for Economic Forecasts

Economists' forecasts typically assume AI is a *one time* event.
: Various assumptoins about speedups across tasks (from @trammell2025workflows):
   
      ![](images/2025-10-23-04-45-32.png){width=7cm}

      @acemoglu2024simple and @aghion2024aigrowth derive growth rates by assuming diffusion speeds.

      But AI capabilities are rapidly increasing -- these areas are expanding.

#  Implication for Economic Forecasts

Much growth is capabilities, not diffusion. 
: Thought experiment: if we had frozen capabilities at gpt4o (May 2024), how much smaller would the impact be today? 

      Some evidence from AB tests on platforms, which compare engagement with different models.

# LLM capabilities are highly correlated

Many studies find high correlations across scores.

: E.g. @ruan2024observational finds the first factor explains 80% of variance: ![](images/image4.png){width=5cm}

: There is also high correlation between scores on benchmarks and scores on user-preference rankings.

# LLM capabilities are highly correlated

What does capability correlation mean concretely?

: The model that is best at math is also probably best at programming, medical advice, legal advice, general knowledge, etc.

      It was not obvious that this would have happened. The best program at chess is not the best program at jeapordy, and vice-versa.

Why should this be so?

: A common interpretation is based on bitter lesson / manifold hypothesis / scaling laws: training a larger model makes it better at everything, by recovering deep latent structure of the world.

Qualifications.
:     1. There is still a tradeoff between *cost* and ability (usually cost and speed are highly correlated).

      1. Different frontier models do have different specialities. However typically any frontier model today will beat *all* frontier models from 6 months ago.

      2. Fine-tuning on proprietary data can make capabilities spiky.

      3. Post-training with RL may induce less correlation.


# Implication: we may not be able to direct technical change

Should we direct AI towards augmenting instead of automating?
: @brynjolfsson2023turing: *"an excessive focus on developing and deploying [human-level AI] can lead us into a trap ... when AI is focused on augmenting humans rather than mimicking them, then humans retain the power to insist on a share of the value created"*

      \   
      @acemoglu2021ai: *"our current trajectory automates work to an excessive degree while refusing to invest in human productivity."*

Our ability to direct change may be limited.

: If there is truly a single latent factor of model ability, then work to train an augmenting model looks very similar to work to train an automating model, & the ability to steer AI capabilities may be limited.


# LLM capabilities are distinct from human capabilities

Ideally we would compare human and LLM performance on the same tasks.

:  If we had a full matrix of human and LLM performance we would be able to compare latent factors of each. Unfortunately there are few datasets which collect human performance across a range of distinct benchmarks. 

Qualitatively, LLM and human abilities appear very different.

:  Aptitude tests that are predictive for humans are not predictive for LLMs. GPT-4 was able to get human-level scores on SAT, LSAT, civil service exams, but not able to do those jobs.

# Implication: a single-factor model will be a poor fit

We sometimes describe AI capability by human equivalent.

: E.g. years of education (@aschenbrenner2024situational)
: ![](images/2025-07-17-07-40-28.png){width=5cm}

Some models assume a common human/AI skill factor.

: E.g. @ide2024artificialintelligenceknowledgeeconomy.

What would a two-factor model look like?

: - LLMs have PhD-level knowledge and reasoning.
: - LLMs have preschool-level tactics.


# There is no consensus on the bottleneck

| Bottleneck                     | Status                                 |
| ------------------------------ | -------------------------------------- |
| Cost.                          | Does not seem an important bottleneck. |
|                                |                                        |
| Deductive reasoning.           | Much improved since 2024.              |
| Information-gathering          | Much improved since 2024.              |
| Accuracy / hallucination.      | Much improved since 2024.              |
| Long context.                  | Much improved since 2024.              |
| Multimodal inputs and outputs. | Much improved since 2024.              |
| In-context learning.           | Much improved since 2024 (ARC-AGI).    |
|                                |                                        |
| Continual learning.            | Amodei, Karpathy, Hasssabis.           |
| Novel situations               | Vafa et al. (2024) on world models.    |
| Interactive decision-making.   | Still struggles.                       |
| Human predictability           | Jagged frontier, Vafa et al. (2024)    |


Note: once a problem has been well-defined, LLMs have a very strong track record of solving it.


# Inference prices are falling at 10X/year

From Artificial Analysis.
: For given capabilities inference prices have been falling at 10X+/year.

      ![](images/2025-10-20-12-31-11.png){width=6cm}

Why are they falling?
: Not because of lower margins -- we see the same trend looking at raw compute cost for open models.

      Smaller models are getting better through (1) better training techniques; (2) more training compute; (3) more training data; (4) better training data.

# LLMs can either do a task cheaply or not at all

Ability to do tasks.
: @metr2024capability say “when agents *can* do a task, they can often do so at a fraction of the cost of humans.” 

      ![](images/image16.png){width=8cm}

Some exceptions to this rule.
: 
      1. Voice transcription for a brief period.
      2. Some reasoning tasks ([ARC-AGI](https://arcprize.org/arc-agi)), briefly.
      3. Fixed costs (@svanberg2024beyond).

# Implication: wages are unlikely to be pinned down by the price of compute

Some models feature equilibrium task-sharing: 
: Humans perform tasks that computers are able to do, but it is too expensive for computers:

      - @trammell2023economic
      - @ide2024artificialintelligenceknowledgeeconomy
      - @smith2024
      - @acemoglu2024simple

Equilibrium task-sharing would require either:

: 1. A dramatic increase in AI prices to perform a task:

       - An increase in the compute required for new tasks (the price of frontier inference has been steady).
       - An increase in compute costs (GPU rental prices have been steady, and the purchase/rent ratio has been stable).
       - An increase in margins.
   
    1. A dramatic drop in human wages.
